Synthetic Data

Throughout the book, we use two simple synthetic data sets to illustrate many of the algorithms. The first of these is a regression problem, based on the sinusoidal function, shown in Figure A.6. The input values {xn}\{ x _ { n } \} are generated uniformly in range (0, 1), and the corresponding target values {tn}\left\{ t _ { n } \right\} are obtained by first computing the corresponding values of the function sin (2πx)( 2 \pi x ) , and then adding random noise with a Gaussian distribution having standard deviation 0.3. Various forms of this data set, having different numbers of data points, are used in the book.

The second data set is a classification problem having two classes, with equal prior probabilities, and is shown in Figure A.7. The blue class is generated from a single Gaussian while the red class comes from a mixture of two Gaussians. Because we know the class priors and the class-conditional densities, it is straightforward to evaluate and plot the true posterior probabilities as well as the minimum misclassification-rate decision boundary, as shown in Figure A.7.

Figure A.6 The left-hand plot shows the synthetic regression data set along with the underlying sinusoidal function from which the data points were generated. The right-hand plot shows the true conditional distribution p(t|x)p ( t | x ) from which the labels are generated, in which the green curve denotes the mean, and the shaded region spans one standard deviation on each side of the mean.

Figure A.7 The left plot shows the synthetic classification data set with data from the two classes shown in red and blue. On the right is a plot of the true posterior probabilities, shown on a colour scale going from pure red denoting probability of the red class is 1 to pure blue denoting probability of the red class is 0. Because these probabilities are known, the optimal decision boundary for minimizing the misclassification rate (which corresponds to the contour along which the posterior probabilities for each class equal 0.5) can be evaluated and is shown by the green curve. This decision boundary is also plotted on the left-hand figure.

Appendix B. Probability Distributions

In this appendix, we summarize the main properties of some of the most widely used probability distributions, and for each distribution we list some key statistics such as the expectation 𝔼[𝐱]\mathbb { E } [ \mathbf { x } ] , the variance (or covariance), the mode, and the entropy H[x]. All of these distributions are members of the exponential family and are widely used as building blocks for more sophisticated probabilistic models.

Bernoulli

This is the distribution for a single binary variable x∈{0,1}x \ \in \ \{ 0 , 1 \} representing, for example, the result of flipping a coin. It is governed by a single continuous parameter μ∈[0,1]\mu \in [ 0 , 1 ] that represents the probability of x=1x = 1

Bern(x|μ)=μx(1−μ)1−x \mathrm{Bern} (x | \mu) = \mu^ {x} (1 - \mu) ^ {1 - x}\tag{B.1}

𝔼[x]=μ \mathbb {E} [ x ] = \mu\tag{B.2}

var⁡[x]=μ(1−μ) \operatorname{var} [ x ] = \mu (1 - \mu)\tag{B.3}

mode⁡[x]={1 if μ≥0.5,0 otherwise \operatorname{mode} [ x ] = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text { if } \mu \geqslant 0. 5, \\ 0 & \text { otherwise } \end{array} \right.\tag{B.4}

H[x]=−μln⁡μ−(1−μ)ln⁡(1−μ). \mathrm{H} [ x ] = - \mu \ln \mu - (1 - \mu) \ln (1 - \mu).\tag{B.5}

The Bernoulli is a special case of the binomial distribution for the case of a single observation. Its conjugate prior for μ\mu is the beta distribution.

Beta

This is a distribution over a continuous variable μ∈[0,1]\mu \in [ 0 , 1 ] , which is often used to represent the probability for some binary event. It is governed by two parameters a and b that are constrained by a>0a > 0 and b>0b > 0 to ensure that the distribution can be normalized.

Beta⁡(μ|a,b)=Γ(a+b)Γ(a)Γ(b)μa−1(1−μ)b−1 \operatorname{Beta} (\mu | a, b) = \frac {\Gamma (a + b)}{\Gamma (a) \Gamma (b)} \mu^ {a - 1} (1 - \mu) ^ {b - 1}\tag{B.6}

𝔼[μ]=aa+b \mathbb {E} [ \mu ] = \frac {a}{a + b}\tag{B.7}

var⁡[μ]=ab(a+b)2(a+b+1) \operatorname{var} [ \mu ] = \frac {a b}{(a + b) ^ {2} (a + b + 1)}\tag{B.8}

mode[μ]=a−1a+b−2. \mathrm{mode} [ \mu ] = \frac {a - 1}{a + b - 2}.\tag{B.9}

The beta is the conjugate prior for the Bernoulli distribution, for which a and b can be interpreted as the effective prior number of observations of x=1x = 1 and x=0x = 0 respectively. Its density is finite if a≥1a \geqslant 1 and b≥1b \geqslant 1 , otherwise there is a singularity at μ=0\mu = 0 and/or μ=1\mu = 1 . For a=b=1a = b = 1 , it reduces to a uniform distribution. The beta distribution is a special case of the K-state Dirichlet distribution for K=2K = 2

Binomial

The binomial distribution gives the probability of observing m occurrences of x=1x = 1 in a set of N samples from a Bernoulli distribution, where the probability of observing x=1x = 1 is μ∈[0,1]\mu \in [ 0 , 1 ]

Bin⁡(m|N,μ)=(Nm)μm(1−μ)N−m \operatorname{Bin} (m | N, \mu) = \binom {N} {m} \mu^ {m} (1 - \mu) ^ {N - m}\tag{B.10}

𝔼[m]=Nμ \mathbb {E} [ m ] = N \mu\tag{B.11}

var⁡[m]=Nμ(1−μ) \operatorname{var} [ m ] = N \mu (1 - \mu)\tag{B.12}

mode[m]=⌊(N+1)μ⌋ \mathrm{mode} [ m ] = \lfloor (N + 1) \mu \rfloor\tag{B.13}

where ⌊(N+1)μ⌋\left\lfloor ( N + 1 ) \mu \right\rfloor denotes the largest integer that is less than or equal to (N+1)μ.( N + 1 ) \mu . and the quantity

(Nm)=N!m!(N−m)! \binom {N} {m} = \frac {N !}{m ! (N - m) !}\tag{B.14}

denotes the number of ways of choosing m objects out of a total of N identical objects. Here m!m ! , pronounced ‘factorial m′m ^ { \prime } , denotes the product m×(m−1)×m \times ( m - 1 ) \times …,×2×1\ldots , \times 2 \times 1 . The particular case of the binomial distribution for N=1N = 1 is known as the Bernoulli distribution, and for large N the binomial distribution is approximately Gaussian. The conjugate prior for μ\mu is the beta distribution.

Dirichlet

The Dirichlet is a multivariate distribution over K random variables 0≤μk≤10 \leqslant \mu _ { k } \leqslant 1 where k=1,…,Kk = 1 , \ldots , K , subject to the constraints

0≤μk≤1,∑k=1Kμk=1. 0 \leqslant \mu_ {k} \leqslant 1, \quad \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \mu_ {k} = 1.\tag{B.15}

Denoting 𝛍=(μ1,…,μK)T\pmb { \mu } = ( \mu _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mu _ { K } ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } and 𝛂∝(α1,…,αK)T\mathbf { \alpha } \propto ( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { K } ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } , we have

Dir⁡(𝛍|𝛂)=C(𝛂)∏k=1Kμkαk−1 \operatorname{Dir} (\boldsymbol {\mu} | \boldsymbol {\alpha}) = C (\boldsymbol {\alpha}) \prod_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \mu_ {k} ^ {\alpha_ {k} - 1}\tag{B.16}

𝔼[μk]=αkα̂ \mathbb {E} [ \mu_ {k} ] = \frac {\alpha_ {k}}{\widehat {\alpha}}\tag{B.17}

var⁡[μk]=αk(α̂−αk)α̂2(α̂+1) \operatorname{var} [ \mu_ {k} ] = \frac {\alpha_ {k} (\widehat {\alpha} - \alpha_ {k})}{\widehat {\alpha} ^ {2} (\widehat {\alpha} + 1)}\tag{B.18}

cov⁡[μjμk]=−αjαkα̂2(α̂+1) \operatorname{cov} [ \mu_ {j} \mu_ {k} ] = - \frac {\alpha_ {j} \alpha_ {k}}{\widehat {\alpha} ^ {2} (\widehat {\alpha} + 1)}\tag{B.19}

mode[μk]=αk−1α̂−K \mathrm{mode} [ \mu_ {k} ] = \frac {\alpha_ {k} - 1}{\widehat {\alpha} - K}\tag{B.20}

𝔼[ln⁡μk]=ψ(αk)−ψ(α̂) \mathbb {E} [ \ln \mu_ {k} ] = \psi (\alpha_ {k}) - \psi (\widehat {\alpha})\tag{B.21}

H[𝛍]=−∑k=1K(αk−1){ψ(αk)−ψ(α̂)}−ln⁡C(𝛂) \mathrm{H} [ \boldsymbol {\mu} ] = - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} (\alpha_ {k} - 1) \left\{\psi (\alpha_ {k}) - \psi (\widehat {\alpha}) \right\} - \ln C (\boldsymbol {\alpha})\tag{B.22}

where

C(𝛂)=Γ(α̂)Γ(α1)⋯Γ(αK) C (\boldsymbol {\alpha}) = \frac {\Gamma (\widehat {\alpha})}{\Gamma (\alpha_ {1}) \cdots \Gamma (\alpha_ {K})}\tag{B.23}

and

α̂=∑k=1Kαk. \widehat {\alpha} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \alpha_ {k}.\tag{B.24}

Here

ψ(a)≡ddaln⁡Γ(a) \psi (a) \equiv \frac {d}{d a} \ln \Gamma (a)\tag{B.25}

is known as the digamma function (Abramowitz and Stegun, 1965). The parameters αk\alpha _ { k } are subject to the constraint αk>0\alpha _ { k } > 0 in order to ensure that the distribution can be normalized.

The Dirichlet forms the conjugate prior for the multinomial distribution and represents a generalization of the beta distribution. In this case, the parameters αk\alpha _ { k } can be interpreted as effective numbers of observations of the corresponding values of the K-dimensional binary observation vector x. As with the beta distribution, the Dirichlet has finite density everywhere provided αk≥1\alpha _ { k } \geqslant 1 for all k.

Gamma

The Gamma is a probability distribution over a positive random variable τ>0\tau > 0 governed by parameters a and bb that are subject to the constraints a>0a > 0 and b>0b > 0 to ensure that the distribution can be normalized.

Gam⁡(τ|a,b)=1Γ(a)baτa−1e−bτ \operatorname{Gam} (\tau | a, b) = \frac {1}{\Gamma (a)} b ^ {a} \tau^ {a - 1} e ^ {- b \tau}\tag{B.26}

𝔼[τ]=ab \mathbb {E} [ \tau ] = \frac {a}{b}\tag{B.27}

var⁡[τ]=ab2 \operatorname{var} [ \tau ] = \frac {a}{b ^ {2}}\tag{B.28}

mode⁡[τ]=a−1b for α≥1 \operatorname{mode} [ \tau ] = \frac {a - 1}{b} \quad \text { for } \alpha \geqslant 1\tag{B.29}

$$ \mathbb {E} [ \ln \tau ] = \psi (a) - \ln b\tag{B.30} $$

$$ \mathrm{H} [ \tau ] = \ln \Gamma (a) - (a - 1) \psi (a) - \ln b + a\tag{B.31} $$

where ψ(⋅)\psi ( \cdot ) is the digamma function defined by (B.25). The gamma distribution is the conjugate prior for the precision (inverse variance) of a univariate Gaussian. For a≥1a \geqslant 1 the density is everywhere finite, and the special case of a=1a = 1 is known as the exponential distribution.

Gaussian

The Gaussian is the most widely used distribution for continuous variables. It is also known as the normal distribution. In the case of a single variable x∈(−∞,∞)x \in ( - \infty , \infty ) it is governed by two parameters, the mean μ∈(−∞,∞)\mu \in ( - \infty , \infty ) and the variance σ2>0\sigma ^ { 2 } > 0

𝒩(x|μ,σ2)=1(2πσ2)1/2exp⁡{−12σ2(x−μ)2} \mathcal {N} (x | \mu , \sigma^ {2}) = \frac {1}{(2 \pi \sigma^ {2}) ^ {1 / 2}} \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {2}} (x - \mu) ^ {2} \right\}\tag{B.32}

𝔼[x]=μ \mathbb {E} [ x ] = \mu\tag{B.33}

var⁡[x]=σ2 \operatorname{var} [ x ] = \sigma^ {2}\tag{B.34}

mode[x]=μ \mathrm{mode} [ x ] = \mu\tag{B.35}

H[x]=12ln⁡σ2+12(1+ln⁡(2π)). \mathrm{H} [ x ] = \frac {1}{2} \ln \sigma^ {2} + \frac {1}{2} (1 + \ln (2 \pi)).\tag{B.36}

The inverse of the variance τ=1/σ2\tau = 1 / \sigma ^ { 2 } is called the precision, and the square root of the variance σ\sigma is called the standard deviation. The conjugate prior for μ\mu is the Gaussian, and the conjugate prior for τ\tau is the gamma distribution. If both μ\mu and τ\tau are unknown, their joint conjugate prior is the Gaussian-gamma distribution.

For a D-dimensional vector x, the Gaussian is governed by a D-dimensional mean vector 𝛍\pmb { \mu } and a D×DD \times D covariance matrix 𝚺\pmb { \Sigma } that must be symmetric and

positive-definite.

𝒩(𝐱|𝛍,𝚺)=1(2π)D/21|𝚺|1/2exp⁡{−12(𝐱−𝛍)T𝚺−1(𝐱−𝛍)} \mathcal {N} (\mathbf {x} | \boldsymbol {\mu}, \boldsymbol {\Sigma}) = \frac {1}{(2 \pi) ^ {D / 2}} \frac {1}{| \boldsymbol {\Sigma} | ^ {1 / 2}} \exp \left\{- \frac {1}{2} (\mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu}) ^ {\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol {\Sigma} ^ {- 1} (\mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu}) \right\}\tag{B.37}

𝔼[𝐱]=𝛍 \mathbb {E} [ \mathbf {x} ] = \boldsymbol {\mu}\tag{B.38}

cov⁡[𝐱]=𝚺 \operatorname{cov} [ \mathbf {x} ] = \boldsymbol {\Sigma}\tag{B.39}

mode[𝐱]=𝛍 \mathrm{mode} [ \mathbf {x} ] = \boldsymbol {\mu}\tag{B.40}

H[𝐱]=12ln⁡|𝚺|+D2(1+ln⁡(2π)). \mathrm{H} [ \mathbf {x} ] = \frac {1}{2} \ln | \boldsymbol {\Sigma} | + \frac {D}{2} (1 + \ln (2 \pi)).\tag{B.41}

The inverse of the covariance matrix 𝚲=𝚺−1\pmb { \Lambda } = \pmb { \Sigma } ^ { - 1 } is the precision matrix, which is also symmetric and positive definite. Averages of random variables tend to a Gaussian, by the central limit theorem, and the sum of two Gaussian variables is again Gaussian. The Gaussian is the distribution that maximizes the entropy for a given variance (or covariance). Any linear transformation of a Gaussian random variable is again Gaussian. The marginal distribution of a multivariate Gaussian with respect to a subset of the variables is itself Gaussian, and similarly the conditional distribution is also Gaussian. The conjugate prior for 𝛍\pmb { \mu } is the Gaussian, the conjugate prior for Λ is the Wishart, and the conjugate prior for (μ,Λ)( \mu , \Lambda ) is the Gaussian-Wishart.

If we have a marginal Gaussian distribution for x and a conditional Gaussian distribution for y given x in the form

p(𝐱)=𝒩(𝐱|𝛍,𝚲−1) {p (\mathbf {x})} = {\mathcal {N} (\mathbf {x} | \boldsymbol {\mu}, \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ^ {- 1})}\tag{B.42}

p(𝐲|𝐱)=𝒩(𝐲|𝐀𝐱+𝐛,𝐋−1) p (\mathbf {y} | \mathbf {x}) = \mathcal {N} (\mathbf {y} | \mathbf {A x} + \mathbf {b}, \mathbf {L} ^ {- 1})\tag{B.43}

then the marginal distribution of 𝐲:\mathbf { y } _ { \mathrm { : } } , and the conditional distribution of x given y, are given by

p(𝐲)=𝒩(𝐲|𝐀𝛍+𝐛,𝐋−1+𝐀𝚲−1𝐀T) {p (\mathbf {y})} = {\mathcal {N} (\mathbf {y} | \mathbf {A} \boldsymbol {\mu} + \mathbf {b}, \mathbf {L} ^ {- 1} + \mathbf {A} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {A} ^ {\mathrm{T}})}\tag{B.44}

p(𝐱|𝐲)=𝒩(𝐱|𝚺{𝐀T𝐋(𝐲−𝐛)+𝚲𝛍},𝚺) {p (\mathbf {x} | \mathbf {y})} = {\mathcal {N} (\mathbf {x} | \boldsymbol {\Sigma} \{\mathbf {A} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {L} (\mathbf {y} - \mathbf {b}) + \boldsymbol {\Lambda} \boldsymbol {\mu} \}, \boldsymbol {\Sigma})}\tag{B.45}

where

𝚺=(𝚲+𝐀T𝐋𝐀)−1. \boldsymbol {\Sigma} = \left(\boldsymbol {\Lambda} + \mathbf {A} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {L} \mathbf {A}\right) ^ {- 1}.\tag{B.46}

If we have a joint Gaussian distribution $\mathcal { N } ( { \bf x } | \mu , \Sigma )$ with 𝚲≡𝚺−1\pmb { \Lambda } \equiv \pmb { \Sigma } ^ { - 1 } and we define the following partitions

𝐱=(𝐱a𝐱b),𝛍=(𝛍a𝛍b) \mathbf {x} = \binom{\mathbf {x} _ {a}}{\mathbf {x} _ {b}}, \quad \boldsymbol {\mu} = \binom{\boldsymbol {\mu} _ {a}}{\boldsymbol {\mu} _ {b}}\tag{B.47}

𝚺=(𝚺aa𝚺ab𝚺ba𝚺bb),𝚲=(𝚲aa𝚲ab𝚲ba𝚲bb) \boldsymbol {\Sigma} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \boldsymbol {\Sigma} _ {a a} & \boldsymbol {\Sigma} _ {a b} \\ \boldsymbol {\Sigma} _ {b a} & \boldsymbol {\Sigma} _ {b b} \end{array} \right), \quad \boldsymbol {\Lambda} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} _ {a a} & \boldsymbol {\Lambda} _ {a b} \\ \boldsymbol {\Lambda} _ {b a} & \boldsymbol {\Lambda} _ {b b} \end{array} \right)\tag{B.48}

then the conditional distribution p(𝐱a|𝐱b)p ( \mathbf { x } _ { a } | \mathbf { x } _ { b } ) is given by

p(𝐱a|𝐱b)=𝒩(𝐱|𝛍a|b,𝚲aa−1) {p (\mathbf {x} _ {a} | \mathbf {x} _ {b})} = {\mathcal {N} (\mathbf {x} | \boldsymbol {\mu} _ {a | b}, \boldsymbol {\Lambda} _ {a a} ^ {- 1})}\tag{B.49}

𝛍a|b=𝛍a−𝚲aa−1𝚲ab(𝐱b−𝛍b) {\pmb {\mu} _ {a | b}} = {\pmb {\mu} _ {a} - \pmb {\Lambda} _ {a a} ^ {- 1} \pmb {\Lambda} _ {a b} (\mathbf {x} _ {b} - \pmb {\mu} _ {b})}\tag{B.50}

and the marginal distribution p(𝐱a)p ( \mathbf { x } _ { a } ) is given by

p(𝐱a)=𝒩(𝐱a|𝛍a,𝚺aa). p (\mathbf {x} _ {a}) = \mathcal {N} (\mathbf {x} _ {a} | \boldsymbol {\mu} _ {a}, \boldsymbol {\Sigma} _ {a a}).\tag{B.51}

Gaussian-Gamma

This is the conjugate prior distribution for a univariate Gaussian 𝒩(𝐱|μ,λ−1)\mathcal { N } ( \boldsymbol { x } | \mu , \lambda ^ { - 1 } ) in which the mean μ\mu and the precision λ are both unknown and is also called the normal-gamma distribution. It comprises the product of a Gaussian distribution for μ,\mu , whose precision is proportional to λ, and a gamma distribution over λ.

p(μ,λ|μ0,β,a,b)=𝒩(μ|μo,(βλ)−1)Gam⁡(λ|a,b). p (\mu , \lambda | \mu_ {0}, \beta , a, b) = \mathcal {N} \left(\mu | \mu_ {o}, (\beta \lambda) ^ {- 1}\right) \operatorname{Gam} (\lambda | a, b).\tag{B.52}

Gaussian-Wishart

This is the conjugate prior distribution for a multivariate Gaussian 𝒩(𝐱|𝛍,𝚲𝚲)\mathcal { N } ( \mathbf { x } | \boldsymbol { \mu } , \mathbf { \Lambda } \mathbf { \Lambda } ) in which both the mean 𝛍\pmb { \mu } and the precision Λ are unknown, and is also called the normal-Wishart distribution. It comprises the product of a Gaussian distribution for μ,\mu , whose precision is proportional to Λ, and a Wishart distribution over Λ.

p(𝛍,𝚲|𝛍0,β,𝐖,ν)=𝒩(𝛍|𝛍0,(β𝚲)−1)𝒲(𝚲|𝐖,ν). p (\boldsymbol {\mu}, \boldsymbol {\Lambda} | \boldsymbol {\mu} _ {0}, \beta , \mathbf {W}, \nu) = \mathcal {N} \left(\boldsymbol {\mu} | \boldsymbol {\mu} _ {0}, (\beta \boldsymbol {\Lambda}) ^ {- 1}\right) \mathcal {W} (\boldsymbol {\Lambda} | \mathbf {W}, \nu).\tag{B.53}

For the particular case of a scalar x, this is equivalent to the Gaussian-gamma distribution.

Multinomial

If we generalize the Bernoulli distribution to an K-dimensional binary variable x with components xk∈{0,1}x _ { k } \in \{ 0 , 1 \} such that ∑kxk=1\textstyle \sum _ { k } x _ { k } = 1 , then we obtain the following discrete distribution

p(𝐱)=∏k=1Kμkxk p (\mathbf {x}) = \prod_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \mu_ {k} ^ {x _ {k}}\tag{B.54}

𝔼[xk]=μk \mathbb {E} [ x _ {k} ] = \mu_ {k}\tag{B.55}

var⁡[xk]=μk(1−μk) \operatorname{var} [ x _ {k} ] = \mu_ {k} (1 - \mu_ {k})\tag{B.56}

cov[xjxk]=Ijkμk {\mathrm{cov} [ x _ {j} x _ {k} ]} = {I _ {j k} \mu_ {k}}\tag{B.57}

H[𝐱]=−∑k=1Mμkln⁡μk \mathrm{H} [ \mathbf {x} ] = - \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {M} \mu_ {k} \ln \mu_ {k}\tag{B.58}

where IjkI _ { j k } is the j,kj , k element of the identity matrix. Because p(xk=1)=μkp ( x _ { k } = 1 ) = \mu _ { k } , the parameters must satisfy 0≤μk≤10 \leqslant \mu _ { k } \leqslant 1 and ∑kμk=1\textstyle \sum _ { k } \mu _ { k } = 1

The multinomial distribution is a multivariate generalization of the binomial and gives the distribution over counts mkm _ { k } for a K-state discrete variable to be in state k given a total number of observations N.

Mult (m1,m2,…,mK|𝛍,N)=(Nm1m2…mM)∏k=1Mμkmk \text { Mult } (m _ {1}, m _ {2}, \ldots , m _ {K} | \boldsymbol {\mu}, N) = \binom{N}{m _ {1} m _ {2} \ldots m _ {M}} \prod_ {k = 1} ^ {M} \mu_ {k} ^ {m _ {k}}\tag{B.59}

𝔼[mk]=Nμk \mathbb {E} [ m _ {k} ] = N \mu_ {k}\tag{B.60}

var[mk]=Nμk(1−μk) {\mathrm{var} [ m _ {k} ]} = {N \mu_ {k} (1 - \mu_ {k})}\tag{B.61}

cov⁡[mjmk]=−Nμjμk \operatorname{cov} [ m _ {j} m _ {k} ] = - N \mu_ {j} \mu_ {k}\tag{B.62}

where 𝛍=(μ1,…,μK)T\pmb { \mu } = ( \mu _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mu _ { K } ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } , and the quantity

(Nm1m2…mK)=N!m1!…mK! \binom {N} {m _ {1} m _ {2} \ldots m _ {K}} = \frac {N !}{m _ {1} ! \ldots m _ {K} !}\tag{B.63}

gives the number of ways of taking N identical objects and assigning mkm _ { k } of them to bin k for k=1,…,Kk = 1 , \ldots , K . The value of μk\mu _ { k } gives the probability of the random variable taking state k, and so these parameters are subject to the constraints 0≤μk≤10 \leqslant \mu _ { k } \leqslant 1 and ∑kμk‾=1\bar { \sum _ { k } \mu _ { k } } ~ = ~ 1 . The conjugate prior distribution for the parameters {μk}\{ \mu _ { k } \} is the Dirichlet.

Normal

The normal distribution is simply another name for the Gaussian. In this book, we use the term Gaussian throughout, although we retain the conventional use of the symbol 𝒩\mathcal { N } to denote this distribution. For consistency, we shall refer to the normalgamma distribution as the Gaussian-gamma distribution, and similarly the normal-Wishart is called the Gaussian-Wishart.

Student’s t

This distribution was published by William Gosset in 1908, but his employer, Guiness Breweries, required him to publish under a pseudonym, so he chose ‘Student’. In the univariate form, Student’s t-distribution is obtained by placing a conjugate gamma prior over the precision of a univariate Gaussian distribution and then integrating out the precision variable. It can therefore be viewed as an infinite mixture of Gaussians having the same mean but different variances.

St⁡(x|μ,λ,ν)=Γ(ν/2+1/2)Γ(ν/2)(λπν)1/2[1+λ(x−μ)2ν]−ν/2−1/2 \operatorname{St} (x | \mu , \lambda , \nu) = \frac {\Gamma (\nu / 2 + 1 / 2)}{\Gamma (\nu / 2)} \left(\frac {\lambda}{\pi \nu}\right) ^ {1 / 2} \left[ 1 + \frac {\lambda (x - \mu) ^ {2}}{\nu} \right] ^ {- \nu / 2 - 1 / 2}\tag{B.64}

𝔼[x]=μforν>1 \mathbb {E} [ x ] = \mu \quad \mathrm{for} \nu > 1\tag{B.65}

var⁡[x]=1λνν−2forν>2 \operatorname{var} [ x ] = \frac {1}{\lambda} \frac {\nu}{\nu - 2} \quad \mathrm{for} \nu > 2\tag{B.66}

mode[x]=μ. \mathrm{mode} [ x ] = \mu .\tag{B.67}

Here ν>0\nu > 0 is called the number of degrees of freedom of the distribution. The particular case of ν=1\nu = 1 is called the Cauchy distribution.

For a D-dimensional variable x, Student’s t-distribution corresponds to marginalizing the precision matrix of a multivariate Gaussian with respect to a conjugate Wishart prior and takes the form

St⁡(𝐱|𝛍,𝚲,ν)=Γ(ν/2+D/2)Γ(ν/2)|𝚲|1/2(νπ)D/2[1+Δ2ν]−ν/2−D/2 \operatorname{St} (\mathbf {x} | \boldsymbol {\mu}, \boldsymbol {\Lambda}, \nu) = \frac {\Gamma (\nu / 2 + D / 2)}{\Gamma (\nu / 2)} \frac {| \boldsymbol {\Lambda} | ^ {1 / 2}}{(\nu \pi) ^ {D / 2}} \left[ 1 + \frac {\Delta^ {2}}{\nu} \right] ^ {- \nu / 2 - D / 2}\tag{B.68}

𝔼[𝐱]=𝛍forν>1 \mathbb {E} [ \mathbf {x} ] = \boldsymbol {\mu} \quad \mathrm{for} \nu > 1\tag{B.69}

cov⁡[𝐱]=νν−2𝚲−1 for ν>2 \operatorname{cov} [ \mathbf {x} ] = \frac {\nu}{\nu - 2} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ^ {- 1} \quad \text { for } \nu > 2\tag{B.70}

mode[𝐱]=𝛍 \mathrm{mode} [ \mathbf {x} ] = \boldsymbol {\mu}\tag{B.71}

where Δ2\Delta ^ { 2 } is the squared Mahalanobis distance defined by

Δ2=(𝐱−𝛍)T𝚲(𝐱−𝛍). \Delta^ {2} = (\mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu}) ^ {\mathrm{T}} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} (\mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu}).\tag{B.72}

In the limit ν→∞\nu \to \infty , the t-distribution reduces to a Gaussian with mean μ\mu and precision Λ. Student’s t-distribution provides a generalization of the Gaussian whose maximum likelihood parameter values are robust to outliers.

Uniform

This is a simple distribution for a continuous variable x defined over a finite interval x∈[a,b]x \in [ a , b ] where b>ab > a

U(x|a,b)=1b−a \mathrm{U} (x | a, b) = \frac {1}{b - a}\tag{B.73}

𝔼[x]=(b+a)2 \mathbb {E} [ x ] = \frac {(b + a)}{2}\tag{B.74}

var⁡[x]=(b−a)212 \operatorname{var} [ x ] = \frac {(b - a) ^ {2}}{1 2}\tag{B.75}

H[x]=ln⁡(b−a). \mathrm{H} [ x ] = \ln (b - a).\tag{B.76}

If x has distribution U(x|0,1)\mathrm { U } ( x | 0 , 1 ) , then a+(b−a)xa + ( b - a ) x will have distribution U(𝐱|𝐚,𝐛)\mathrm { U } ( { \boldsymbol { x } } | { \boldsymbol { a } } , { \boldsymbol { b } } )

Von Mises

The von Mises distribution, also known as the circular normal or the circular Gaussian, is a univariate Gaussian-like periodic distribution for a variable θ∈[0,2π)\theta \in [ 0 , 2 \pi )

p(θ|θ0,m)=12πI0(m)exp⁡{mcos⁡(θ−θ0)} {p (\theta | \theta_ {0}, m)} = {\frac {1}{2 \pi I _ {0} (m)} \exp \{m \cos (\theta - \theta_ {0}) \}}\tag{B.77}

where I0(m)I _ { 0 } ( m ) is the zeroth-order Bessel function of the first kind. The distribution has period 2π2 \pi so that p(θ+2π)=p(θ)p ( \theta + 2 \pi ) = p ( \theta ) for all θ. Care must be taken in interpreting this distribution because simple expectations will be dependent on the (arbitrary) choice of origin for the variable θ. The parameter θ0\theta _ { 0 } is analogous to the mean of a univariate Gaussian, and the parameter m>0m > 0 , known as the concentration parameter, is analogous to the precision (inverse variance). For large m, the von Mises distribution is approximately a Gaussian centred on θ0\theta _ { 0 }

Wishart

The Wishart distribution is the conjugate prior for the precision matrix of a multivariate Gaussian.

𝒲(𝚲|𝐖,ν)=B(𝐖,ν)|𝚲|(ν−D−1)/2exp⁡(−12Tr(𝐖−1𝚲)) \mathcal {W} (\boldsymbol {\Lambda} | \mathbf {W}, \nu) = B (\mathbf {W}, \nu) | \boldsymbol {\Lambda} | ^ {(\nu - D - 1) / 2} \exp \left(- \frac {1}{2} \operatorname{Tr} \left(\mathbf {W} ^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {\Lambda}\right)\right)\tag{B.78}

where

B(𝐖,ν)≡|𝐖|−ν/2(2νD/2πD(D−1)/4∏i=1DΓ(ν+1−i2))−1 B (\mathbf {W}, \nu) \equiv | \mathbf {W} | ^ {- \nu / 2} \left(2 ^ {\nu D / 2} \pi^ {D (D - 1) / 4} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {D} \Gamma \left(\frac {\nu + 1 - i}{2}\right)\right) ^ {- 1}\tag{B.79}

𝔼[𝚲]=ν𝐖 \mathbb {E} [ \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ] = \nu \mathbf {W}\tag{B.80}

𝔼[ln|𝚲|]=∑i=1Dψ(ν+1−i2)+Dln⁡2+ln⁡|𝐖| \mathbb {E} \left[ \ln | \boldsymbol {\Lambda} | \right] = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {D} \psi \left(\frac {\nu + 1 - i}{2}\right) + D \ln 2 + \ln | \mathbf {W} |\tag{B.81}

H[𝚲]=−ln⁡B(𝐖,ν)−(ν−D−1)2𝔼[ln|𝚲|]+νD2 \mathrm{H} [ \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ] = - \ln B (\mathbf {W}, \nu) - \frac {(\nu - D - 1)}{2} \mathbb {E} \left[ \ln | \boldsymbol {\Lambda} | \right] + \frac {\nu D}{2}\tag{B.82}

where W is a D×DD \times D symmetric, positive definite matrix, and ψ(⋅)\psi ( \cdot ) is the digamma function defined by (B.25). The parameter ν is called the number of degrees of freedom of the distribution and is restricted to ν>D−1\nu > D - 1 to ensure that the Gamma function in the normalization factor is well-defined. In one dimension, the Wishart reduces to the gamma distribution Gam(λ|a,b){ \mathrm { G a m } } ( \lambda | a , b ) given by (B.26) with parameters a=ν/2a = \nu / 2 and b=1/2Wb = 1 / 2 W

Appendix C. Properties of Matrices

In this appendix, we gather together some useful properties and identities involving matrices and determinants. This is not intended to be an introductory tutorial, and it is assumed that the reader is already familiar with basic linear algebra. For some results, we indicate how to prove them, whereas in more complex cases we leave the interested reader to refer to standard textbooks on the subject. In all cases, we assume that inverses exist and that matrix dimensions are such that the formulae are correctly defined. A comprehensive discussion of linear algebra can be found in Golub and Van Loan (1996), and an extensive collection of matrix properties is given by Lutkepohl (1996). Matrix derivatives are discussed in Magnus and Neudecker¨ (1999).

Basic Matrix Identities

A matrix A has elements AijA _ { i j } where i indexes the rows, and j indexes the columns. We use 𝐈N{ \mathbf { I } } _ { N } to denote the N×NN \times N identity matrix (also called the unit matrix), and where there is no ambiguity over dimensionality we simply use I. The transpose matrix ${ \bf A } ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ has elements (𝐀T)ij=Aji( \mathbf { A } ^ { \mathrm { T } } ) _ { i j } = A _ { j i } . From the definition of transpose, we have

(𝐀𝐁)T=𝐁T𝐀T (\mathbf {A B}) ^ {\mathrm{T}} = \mathbf {B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {A} ^ {\mathrm{T}}\tag{C.1}

which can be verified by writing out the indices. The inverse of A, denoted 𝐀−1\mathbf { A } ^ { - 1 } satisfies

𝐀𝐀−1=𝐀−1𝐀=𝐈. \mathbf {A} \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} = \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {A} = \mathbf {I}.\tag{C.2}

Because 𝐀𝐁𝐁−1𝐀−1=𝐈\mathbf { A } \mathbf { B } \mathbf { B } ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { A } ^ { - 1 } = \mathbf { I } , we have

(𝐀𝐁)−1=𝐁−1𝐀−1. (\mathbf {A B}) ^ {- 1} = \mathbf {B} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1}.\tag{C.3}

Also we have

(𝐀T)−1=(𝐀−1)T \left(\mathbf {A} ^ {\mathrm{T}}\right) ^ {- 1} = \left(\mathbf {A} ^ {- 1}\right) ^ {\mathrm{T}}\tag{C.4}

which is easily proven by taking the transpose of (C.2) and applying (C.1).

A useful identity involving matrix inverses is the following

(𝐏−1+𝐁T𝐑−1𝐁)−1𝐁T𝐑−1=𝐏𝐁T(𝐁𝐏𝐁T+𝐑)−1. (\mathbf {P} ^ {- 1} + \mathbf {B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {R} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {B}) ^ {- 1} \mathbf {B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {R} ^ {- 1} = \mathbf {P B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} (\mathbf {B P B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} + \mathbf {R}) ^ {- 1}.\tag{C.5}

which is easily verified by right multiplying both sides by (𝐁𝐏𝐁T+𝐑)( \mathbf { B P B ^ { \mathrm { T } } + R } ) . Suppose that P has dimensionality N×NN \times N while R has dimensionality M×MM \times M , so that B is M×NM \times N . Then if M≪NM \ll N , it will be much cheaper to evaluate the right-hand side of (C.5) than the left-hand side. A special case that sometimes arises is

(𝐈+𝐀𝐁)−1𝐀=𝐀(𝐈+𝐁𝐀)−1. (\mathbf {I} + \mathbf {A B}) ^ {- 1} \mathbf {A} = \mathbf {A} (\mathbf {I} + \mathbf {B A}) ^ {- 1}.\tag{C.6}

Another useful identity involving inverses is the following:

(𝐀+𝐁𝐃−1𝐂)−1=𝐀−1−𝐀−1𝐁(𝐃+𝐂𝐀−1𝐁)−1𝐂𝐀−1 (\mathbf {A} + \mathbf {B D} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {C}) ^ {- 1} = \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} - \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {B} (\mathbf {D} + \mathbf {C A} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {B}) ^ {- 1} \mathbf {C A} ^ {- 1}\tag{C.7}

which is known as the Woodbury identity and which can be verified by multiplying both sides by (𝐀+𝐁𝐃−𝟏𝐂)\mathbf { \left( A + B D ^ { - 1 } C \right) } This is useful, for instance, when A is large and diagonal, and hence easy to invert, while B has many rows but few columns (and conversely for C) so that the right-hand side is much cheaper to evaluate than the left-hand side.

A set of vectors {𝐚1,…,𝐚N}\left\{ \mathbf { a } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mathbf { a } _ { N } \right\} is said to be linearly independent if the relation ∑nαn𝐚n=0\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \alpha _ { n } \mathbf { a } _ { n } \ = \ 0 } \end{array} holds only if all αn=0\alpha _ { n } \ = \ 0 . This implies that none of the vectors can be expressed as a linear combination of the remainder. The rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent rows (or equivalently the maximum number of linearly independent columns).

Traces and Determinants

Trace and determinant apply to square matrices. The trace Tr⁡(𝐀)\operatorname { T r } ( \mathbf { A } ) of a matrix A is defined as the sum of the elements on the leading diagonal. By writing out the indices, we see that

Tr⁡(𝐀𝐁)=Tr⁡(𝐁𝐀). \operatorname{Tr} (\mathbf {A B}) = \operatorname{Tr} (\mathbf {B A}).\tag{C.8}

By applying this formula multiple times to the product of three matrices, we see that

Tr⁡(𝐀𝐁𝐂)=Tr⁡(𝐂𝐀𝐁)=Tr⁡(𝐁𝐂𝐀) \operatorname{Tr} (\mathbf {A B C}) = \operatorname{Tr} (\mathbf {C A B}) = \operatorname{Tr} (\mathbf {B C A})\tag{C.9}

which is known as the cyclic property of the trace operator and which clearly extends to the product of any number of matrices. The determinant |𝐀|| \mathbf { A } | of an N×NN \times N matrix A is defined by

|𝐀|=∑(±1)A1i1A2i2…ANiN | \mathbf {A} | = \sum (\pm 1) A _ {1 i _ {1}} A _ {2 i _ {2}} \dots A _ {N i _ {N}}\tag{C.10}

in which the sum is taken over all products consisting of precisely one element from each row and one element from each column, with a coefficient +1 or 1 according to whether the permutation i1i2…iNi _ { 1 } i _ { 2 } \dots i _ { N } is even or odd, respectively. Note that |𝐈|=1| \mathbf { I } | = 1 Thus, for a 2×22 \times 2 matrix, the determinant takes the form

|𝐀|=|a11a12a21a22|=a11a22−a12a21. | \mathbf {A} | = \left| \begin{array}{l l} a _ {1 1} & a _ {1 2} \\ a _ {2 1} & a _ {2 2} \end{array} \right| = a _ {1 1} a _ {2 2} - a _ {1 2} a _ {2 1}.\tag{C.11}

The determinant of a product of two matrices is given by

|𝐀𝐁|=|𝐀||𝐁| | \mathbf {A B} | = | \mathbf {A} | | \mathbf {B} |\tag{C.12}

as can be shown from (C.10). Also, the determinant of an inverse matrix is given by

|𝐀−1|=1|𝐀| \left| \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} \right| = \frac {1}{\left| \mathbf {A} \right|}\tag{C.13}

which can be shown by taking the determinant of (C.2) and applying (C.12).

If A and B are matrices of size N×MN \times M , then

|𝐈N+𝐀𝐁T|=|𝐈M+𝐀T𝐁|. \left| \mathbf {I} _ {N} + \mathbf {A B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \right| = \left| \mathbf {I} _ {M} + \mathbf {A} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {B} \right|.\tag{C.14}

A useful special case is

|𝐈N+𝐚𝐛T|=1+𝐚T𝐛 \left| \mathbf {I} _ {N} + \mathbf {a b} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \right| = 1 + \mathbf {a} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {b}\tag{C.15}

where a and b are N-dimensional column vectors.

Matrix Derivatives

Sometimes we need to consider derivatives of vectors and matrices with respect to scalars. The derivative of a vector a with respect to a scalar x is itself a vector whose components are given by

(∂𝐚∂x)i=∂ai∂x \left(\frac {\partial \mathbf {a}}{\partial x}\right) _ {i} = \frac {\partial a _ {i}}{\partial x}\tag{C.16}

with an analogous definition for the derivative of a matrix. Derivatives with respect to vectors and matrices can also be defined, for instance

(∂x∂𝐚)i=∂x∂ai \left(\frac {\partial x}{\partial \mathbf {a}}\right) _ {i} = \frac {\partial x}{\partial a _ {i}}\tag{C.17}

and similarly

(∂𝐚∂𝐛)ij=∂ai∂bj. \left(\frac {\partial \mathbf {a}}{\partial \mathbf {b}}\right) _ {i j} = \frac {\partial a _ {i}}{\partial b _ {j}}.\tag{C.18}

The following is easily proven by writing out the components

∂∂𝐱(𝐱T𝐚)=∂∂𝐱(𝐚T𝐱)=𝐚. \frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {x}} \left(\mathbf {x} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {a}\right) = \frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {x}} \left(\mathbf {a} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {x}\right) = \mathbf {a}.\tag{C.19}

Similarly

∂∂𝐱(𝐀𝐁)=∂𝐀∂𝐱𝐁+𝐀∂𝐁∂𝐱. \frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {x}} (\mathbf {A B}) = \frac {\partial \mathbf {A}}{\partial \mathbf {x}} \mathbf {B} + \mathbf {A} \frac {\partial \mathbf {B}}{\partial \mathbf {x}}.\tag{C.20}

The derivative of the inverse of a matrix can be expressed as

∂∂x(𝐀−1)=−𝐀−1∂𝐀∂x𝐀−1 \frac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\mathbf {A} ^ {- 1}\right) = - \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} \frac {\partial \mathbf {A}}{\partial x} \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1}\tag{C.21}

as can be shown by differentiating the equation 𝐀−1𝐀=𝐈\mathbf { A } ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { A } = \mathbf { I } using (C.20) and then right multiplying by ${ { \bf A } ^ { - 1 } }$ . Also

∂∂xln⁡|𝐀|=Tr⁡(𝐀−1∂𝐀∂x) \frac {\partial}{\partial x} \ln | \mathbf {A} | = \operatorname{Tr} \left(\mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} \frac {\partial \mathbf {A}}{\partial x}\right)\tag{C.22}

which we shall prove later. If we choose x to be one of the elements of A, we have

∂∂AijTr(𝐀𝐁)=Bji \frac {\partial}{\partial A _ {i j}} \mathrm{Tr} (\mathbf {A B}) = B _ {j i}\tag{C.23}

as can be seen by writing out the matrices using index notation. We can write this result more compactly in the form

∂∂𝐀Tr(𝐀𝐁)=𝐁T. \frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {A}} \mathrm{Tr} (\mathbf {A B}) = \mathbf {B} ^ {\mathrm{T}}.\tag{C.24}

With this notation, we have the following properties

∂∂𝐀Tr(𝐀T𝐁)=𝐁 \frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {A}} \mathrm{Tr} \left(\mathbf {A} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {B}\right) = \mathbf {B}\tag{C.25}

∂∂𝐀Tr(𝐀)=𝐈 {\frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {A}} \mathrm{Tr} (\mathbf {A})} = {\mathbf {I}}\tag{C.26}

∂∂𝐀Tr(𝐀𝐁𝐀T)=𝐀(𝐁+𝐁T) \frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {A}} \mathrm{Tr} (\mathbf {A B A} ^ {\mathrm{T}}) = \mathbf {A} (\mathbf {B} + \mathbf {B} ^ {\mathrm{T}})\tag{C.27}

which can again be proven by writing out the matrix indices. We also have

∂∂𝐀ln⁡|𝐀|=(𝐀−1)T \frac {\partial}{\partial \mathbf {A}} \ln | \mathbf {A} | = (\mathbf {A} ^ {- 1}) ^ {\mathrm{T}}\tag{C.28}

which follows from (C.22) and (C.26).

Eigenvector Equation

For a square matrix A of size M×MM \times M , the eigenvector equation is defined by

𝐀𝐮i=λi𝐮i \mathbf {A} \mathbf {u} _ {i} = \lambda_ {i} \mathbf {u} _ {i}\tag{C.29}

for i=1,…,Mi = 1 , \ldots , M , where 𝐮i\mathbf { u } _ { i } is an eigenvector and λi\lambda _ { i } is the corresponding eigenvalue. This can be viewed as a set of M simultaneous homogeneous linear equations, and the condition for a solution is that

|𝐀−λi𝐈|=0 | \mathbf {A} - \lambda_ {i} \mathbf {I} | = 0\tag{C.30}

which is known as the characteristic equation. Because this is a polynomial of order M in λi.\lambda _ { i } . , it must have M solutions (though these need not all be distinct). The rank of A is equal to the number of nonzero eigenvalues.

Of particular interest are symmetric matrices, which arise as covariance matrices, kernel matrices, and Hessians. Symmetric matrices have the property that Aij=AjiA _ { i j } = A _ { j i } , or equivalently 𝐀T=𝐀\mathbf { A } ^ { \mathrm { T } } = \mathbf { A } . The inverse of a symmetric matrix is also symmetric, as can be seen by taking the transpose of 𝐀−1𝐀̇=𝐈\mathbf { A } ^ { - 1 } \dot { \mathbf { A } } = \mathbf { I } and using 𝐀𝐀−1=𝐈\mathbf { A } \mathbf { A } ^ { - 1 } = \mathbf { I } together with the symmetry of I.

In general, the eigenvalues of a matrix are complex numbers, but for symmetric matrices the eigenvalues λi\lambda _ { i } are real. This can be seen by first left multiplying (C.29) by (𝐮i⋆)T( \mathbf { u } _ { i } ^ { \star } ) ^ { \mathrm { T } } , where denotes the complex conjugate, to give

(𝐮i⋆)T𝐀𝐮i=λi(𝐮i⋆)T𝐮i. \left(\mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\star}\right) ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {A u} _ {i} = \lambda_ {i} \left(\mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\star}\right) ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {u} _ {i}.\tag{C.31}

Next we take the complex conjugate of (C.29) and left multiply by 𝐮iT{ \mathbf { u } } _ { i } ^ { \mathrm { T } } to give

𝐮iT𝐀𝐮i⋆=λi⋆𝐮iT𝐮i⋆. \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {A} \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\star} = \lambda_ {i} ^ {\star} \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\star}.\tag{C.32}

where we have used 𝐀⋆=𝐀\mathbf { A } ^ { \star } = \mathbf { A } because we consider only real matrices A. Taking the transpose of the second of these equations, and using 𝐀T=𝐀\mathbf { A } ^ { \mathrm { T } } = \mathbf { A } , we see that the left-hand sides of the two equations are equal, and hence that λi⋆=λi\lambda _ { i } ^ { \star } = \lambda _ { i } and so λi\lambda _ { i } must be real.

The eigenvectors 𝐮i\mathbf { u } _ { i } of a real symmetric matrix can be chosen to be orthonormal (i.e., orthogonal and of unit length) so that

𝐮iT𝐮j=Iij \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {u} _ {j} = I _ {i j}\tag{C.33}

where IijI _ { i j } are the elements of the identity matrix I. To show this, we first left multiply (C.29) by 𝐮jT\mathbf { u } _ { j } ^ { \mathrm { T } } to give

𝐮jT𝐀𝐮i=λi𝐮jT𝐮i \mathbf {u} _ {j} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {A} \mathbf {u} _ {i} = \lambda_ {i} \mathbf {u} _ {j} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {u} _ {i}\tag{C.34}

and hence, by exchange of indices, we have

𝐮iT𝐀𝐮j=λj𝐮iT𝐮j. \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {A} \mathbf {u} _ {j} = \lambda_ {j} \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {u} _ {j}.\tag{C.35}

We now take the transpose of the second equation and make use of the symmetry property 𝐀T=𝐀\mathbf { A } ^ { \mathrm { T } } = \mathbf { A } , and then subtract the two equations to give

(λi−λj)𝐮iT𝐮j=0. \left(\lambda_ {i} - \lambda_ {j}\right) \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {u} _ {j} = 0.\tag{C.36}

Hence, for λi≠λj\lambda _ { i } \neq \lambda _ { j } , we have 𝐮iT𝐮j=0\mathbf { u } _ { i } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \mathbf { u } _ { j } = 0 , and hence 𝐮i\mathbf { u } _ { i } and 𝐮j\mathbf { u } _ { j } are orthogonal. If the two eigenvalues are equal, then any linear combination α𝐮i+β𝐮j\alpha \mathbf { u } _ { i } + \beta \mathbf { u } _ { j } is also an eigenvector with the same eigenvalue, so we can select one linear combination arbitrarily, and then choose the second to be orthogonal to the first (it can be shown that the degenerate eigenvectors are never linearly dependent). Hence the eigenvectors can be chosen to be orthogonal, and by normalizing can be set to unit length. Because there are M eigenvalues, the corresponding M orthogonal eigenvectors form a complete set and so any M-dimensional vector can be expressed as a linear combination of the eigenvectors.

We can take the eigenvectors 𝐮i\mathbf { u } _ { i } to be the columns of an M×MM \times M matrix U, which from orthonormality satisfies

𝐔T𝐔=𝐈. \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {U} = \mathbf {I}.\tag{C.37}

Such a matrix is said to be orthogonal. Interestingly, the rows of this matrix are also orthogonal, so that 𝐔𝐔T=𝐈\mathbf { U } \mathbf { U } ^ { \mathrm { T } } = \mathbf { I } . To show this, note that (C.37) implies $\begin{array} { r } { { \bf U } ^ { \mathrm { T } } { \bf U } { \bf U } ^ { - 1 } = \qquad } \end{array}$ 𝐔−1=𝐔T\mathbf { U } ^ { - 1 } = \mathbf { U } ^ { \mathrm { T } } and so 𝐔𝐔−1=𝐔𝐔T=𝐈.\mathbf { U U } ^ { - 1 } = \mathbf { U U } ^ { \mathrm { T } } = \mathbf { I } . . Using (C.12), it also follows that |𝐔|=1| \mathbf { U } | = 1 The eigenvector equation (C.29) can be expressed in terms of U in the form The eigenvector equation (C.29) can be expressed in terms of U in the form

𝐀𝐔=𝐔𝚲 \mathbf {A} \mathbf {U} = \mathbf {U} \boldsymbol {\Lambda}\tag{C.38}

where Λ is an M×MM \times M diagonal matrix whose diagonal elements are given by the eigenvalues λi\lambda _ { i }

If we consider a column vector x that is transformed by an orthogonal matrix U to give a new vector

𝐱̃=𝐔𝐱 \widetilde {\mathbf {x}} = \mathbf {U} \mathbf {x}\tag{C.39}

then the length of the vector is preserved because

𝐱̃T𝐱̃=𝐱T𝐔T𝐔𝐱=𝐱T𝐱 \widetilde {\mathbf {x}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \widetilde {\mathbf {x}} = \mathbf {x} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {U} \mathbf {x} = \mathbf {x} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {x}\tag{C.40}

and similarly the angle between any two such vectors is preserved because

𝐱̃T𝐲̃=𝐱T𝐔T𝐔𝐲=𝐱T𝐲. \widetilde {\mathbf {x}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \widetilde {\mathbf {y}} = \mathbf {x} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {U} \mathbf {y} = \mathbf {x} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {y}.\tag{C.41}

Thus, multiplication by U can be interpreted as a rigid rotation of the coordinate system.

From (C.38), it follows that

𝐔T𝐀𝐔=𝚲 \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {A} \mathbf {U} = \boldsymbol {\Lambda}\tag{C.42}

and because Λ is a diagonal matrix, we say that the matrix A is diagonalized by the matrix U. If we left multiply by U and right multiply by 𝐔T\mathbf { U } ^ { \mathrm { T } } , we obtain

𝐀=𝐔𝚲𝐔T \mathbf {A} = \mathbf {U} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{T}}\tag{C.43}

Taking the inverse of this equation, and using (C.3) together with 𝐔−1=𝐔T\mathbf { U } ^ { - 1 } = \mathbf { U } ^ { \mathrm { T } } , we have

𝐀−1=𝐔𝚲−1𝐔T. \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} = \mathbf {U} \boldsymbol {\Lambda} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{T}}.\tag{C.44}

These last two equations can also be written in the form

𝐀=∑i=1Mλi𝐮i𝐮iT \mathbf {A} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {M} \lambda_ {i} \mathbf {u} _ {i} \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}}\tag{C.45}

𝐀−1=∑i=1M1λi𝐮i𝐮iT. \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {M} \frac {1}{\lambda_ {i}} \mathbf {u} _ {i} \mathbf {u} _ {i} ^ {\mathrm{T}}.\tag{C.46}

If we take the determinant of (C.43), and use (C.12), we obtain

|𝐀|=∏i=1Mλi. | \mathbf {A} | = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {M} \lambda_ {i}.\tag{C.47}

Similarly, taking the trace of (C.43), and using the cyclic property (C.8) of the trace operator together with 𝐔T𝐔=𝐈\mathbf { U } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \mathbf { U } = \mathbf { I } , we have

Tr⁡(𝐀)=∑i=1Mλi. \operatorname{Tr} (\mathbf {A}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {M} \lambda_ {i}.\tag{C.48}

We leave it as an exercise for the reader to verify (C.22) by making use of the results (C.33), (C.45), (C.46), and (C.47).

A matrix A is said to be positive definite, denoted by 𝐀≻0\mathbf A \succ 0 , if 𝐰T𝐀𝐰>0\mathbf { w } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { w } > 0 for all values of the vector w. Equivalently, a positive definite matrix has λi>0\lambda _ { i } > 0 for all of its eigenvalues (as can be seen by setting w to each of the eigenvectors in turn, and by noting that an arbitrary vector can be expanded as a linear combination of the eigenvectors). Note that positive definite is not the same as all the elements being positive. For example, the matrix

(1234) \left( \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right)\tag{C.49}

has eigenvalues λ1≃5.37\lambda _ { 1 } \simeq 5 . 3 7 and λ2≃−0.37\lambda _ { 2 } \simeq - 0 . 3 7 . A matrix is said to be positive semidefinite if 𝐰T𝐀𝐰≥0\mathbf { w } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { w } \ \geqslant \ 0 holds for all values of w, which is denoted 𝐀 ≽0\textbf { A } \succeq 0 , and is equivalent to λi≥0\lambda _ { i } \geqslant 0

Appendix D. Calculus of Variations

We can think of a function y(x)y ( x ) as being an operator that, for any input value x,x , returns an output value y.y . In the same way, we can define a functional F[y]F [ y ] to be an operator that takes a function y(x)y ( x ) and returns an output value F.F . . An example of a functional is the length of a curve drawn in a two-dimensional plane in which the path of the curve is defined in terms of a function. In the context of machine learning, a widely used functional is the entropy H[x]\mathrm { H } [ x ] for a continuous variable x because, for any choice of probability density function p(x)p ( x ) , it returns a scalar value representing the entropy of x under that density. Thus the entropy of p(x)p ( x ) could equally well have been written as H[p]\mathrm { H } [ p ]

A common problem in conventional calculus is to find a value of xx that maximizes (or minimizes) a function y(x)y ( x ) . Similarly, in the calculus of variations we seek a function y(x)y ( x ) that maximizes (or minimizes) a functional F[y]F [ y ] . That is, of all possible functions y(x)y ( x ) , we wish to find the particular function for which the functional F[y]F [ y ] is a maximum (or minimum). The calculus of variations can be used, for instance, to show that the shortest path between two points is a straight line or that the maximum entropy distribution is a Gaussian.

If we weren’t familiar with the rules of ordinary calculus, we could evaluate a conventional derivative dy/\mathrm { d } y / dx by making a small change to the variable x and then expanding in powers of , so that

y(x+ϵ)=y(x)+dydxϵ+O(ϵ2) y (x + \epsilon) = y (x) + \frac {\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x} \epsilon + O (\epsilon^ {2})\tag{D.1}

and finally taking the limit ϵ0.\epsilon 0 . . Similarly, for a function of several variables y(x1,…,xD)y ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { D } ) , the corresponding partial derivatives are defined by

y(x1+ϵ1,…,xD+ϵD)=y(x1,…,xD)+∑i=1D∂y∂xiϵi+O(ϵ2). y (x _ {1} + \epsilon_ {1}, \dots , x _ {D} + \epsilon_ {D}) = y (x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {D}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {D} \frac {\partial y}{\partial x _ {i}} \epsilon_ {i} + O (\epsilon^ {2}).\tag{D.2}

The analogous definition of a functional derivative arises when we consider how much a functional F[y]F [ y ] changes when we make a small change ϵη(x)\epsilon \eta ( x ) to the function

Figure D.1 A functional derivative can be defined by considering how the value of a functional F[y]F [ y ] changes when the function y(x)y ( x ) is changed to y(x)+ϵη(x)y ( x ) + \epsilon \eta ( x ) where η(x)\eta ( x ) is an arbitrary function of x.

y(x)y ( x ) , where η(x)\eta ( x ) is an arbitrary function of x,x , , as illustrated in Figure D.1. We denote the functional derivative of E[f]E [ f ] with respect to f(x)f ( x ) by δF/δf(x)\delta F / \delta f ( x ) , and define it by the following relation:

F[y(x)+ϵη(x)]=F[y(x)]+ϵ∫δFδy(x)η(x)dx+O(ϵ2). F [ y (x) + \epsilon \eta (x) ] = F [ y (x) ] + \epsilon \int \frac {\delta F}{\delta y (x)} \eta (x) \mathrm{d} x + O (\epsilon^ {2}).\tag{D.3}

This can be seen as a natural extension of (D.2) in which F[y]F [ y ] now depends on a continuous set of variables, namely the values of yy at all points x. Requiring that the functional be stationary with respect to small variations in the function y(x)y ( x ) gives

∫δEδy(x)η(x)dx=0. \int {\frac {\delta E}{\delta y (x)}} \eta (x) \mathrm{d} x = 0.\tag{D.4}

Because this must hold for an arbitrary choice of η(x)\eta ( x ) , it follows that the functional derivative must vanish. To see this, imagine choosing a perturbation η(x)\eta ( x ) that is zero everywhere except in the neighbourhood of a point x̂,{ \widehat { x } } , in which case the functional derivative must be zero at x=x̂x = { \widehat { x } } However, because this must be true for every choice of x̂.{ \widehat { x } } . , the functional derivative must vanish for all values of x.x .

Consider a functional that is defined by an integral over a function G(y,y′,x)G ( y , y ^ { \prime } , x ) that depends on both y(x)y ( x ) and its derivative y′(x)y ^ { \prime } ( x ) as well as having a direct dependence on x

$$ F [ y ] = \int G (y (x), y ^ {\prime} (x), x) \mathrm{d} x\tag{D.5} $$

where the value of y(x)y ( x ) is assumed to be fixed at the boundary of the region of integration (which might be at infinity). If we now consider variations in the function y(x)y ( x ) , we obtain

F[y(x)+ϵη(x)]=F[y(x)]+ϵ∫{∂G∂yη(x)+∂G∂y′η′(x)}dx+O(ϵ2). F [ y (x) + \epsilon \eta (x) ] = F [ y (x) ] + \epsilon \int \left\{\frac {\partial G}{\partial y} \eta (x) + \frac {\partial G}{\partial y ^ {\prime}} \eta^ {\prime} (x) \right\} d x + O (\epsilon^ {2}).\tag{D.6}

We now have to cast this in the form (D.3). To do so, we integrate the second term by parts and make use of the fact that η(x)\eta ( x ) must vanish at the boundary of the integral (because y(x)y ( x ) is fixed at the boundary). This gives

F[y(x)+ϵη(x)]=F[y(x)]+ϵ∫{∂G∂y−ddx(∂G∂y′)}η(x)dx+O(ϵ2) F [ y (x) + \epsilon \eta (x) ] = F [ y (x) ] + \epsilon \int \left\{\frac {\partial G}{\partial y} - \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} \left(\frac {\partial G}{\partial y ^ {\prime}}\right) \right\} \eta (x) \mathrm{d} x + O (\epsilon^ {2})\tag{D.7}

from which we can read off the functional derivative by comparison with (D.3). Requiring that the functional derivative vanishes then gives

∂G∂y−ddx(∂G∂y′)=0 \frac {\partial G}{\partial y} - \frac {\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} \left(\frac {\partial G}{\partial y ^ {\prime}}\right) = 0\tag{D.8}

which are known as the Euler-Lagrange equations. For example, if

G=y(x)2+(y′(x))2 G = y (x) ^ {2} + \left(y ^ {\prime} (x)\right) ^ {2}\tag{D.9}

then the Euler-Lagrange equations take the form

y(x)−d2ydx2=0. y (x) - \frac {\mathrm{d} ^ {2} y}{\mathrm{d} x ^ {2}} = 0.\tag{D.10}

This second order differential equation can be solved for y(x)y ( x ) by making use of the boundary conditions on y(x)y ( x )

Often, we consider functionals defined by integrals whose integrands take the form G(y,x)G ( y , x ) and that do not depend on the derivatives of y(x)y ( x ) . In this case, stationarity simply requires that ∂G/∂y(x)=0\partial G / \partial y ( x ) = 0 for all values of xx .

If we are optimizing a functional with respect to a probability distribution, then we need to maintain the normalization constraint on the probabilities. This is often most conveniently done using a Lagrange multiplier, which then allows an unconstrained optimization to be performed.

The extension of the above results to a multidimensional variable x is straightforward. For a more comprehensive discussion of the calculus of variations, see Sagan (1969).

Appendix E. Lagrange Multipliers

Lagrange multipliers, also sometimes called undetermined multipliers, are used to find the stationary points of a function of several variables subject to one or more constraints.

Consider the problem of finding the maximum of a function f(x1,x2)f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) subject to a constraint relating x1x _ { 1 } and x2x _ { 2 } , which we write in the form

g(x1,x2)=0. g (x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = 0.\tag{E.1}

One approach would be to solve the constraint equation (E.1) and thus express x2x _ { 2 } as a function of x1x _ { 1 } in the form x2=h(x1)x _ { 2 } = h ( x _ { 1 } ) . This can then be substituted into f(x1,x2)f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) to give a function of x1x _ { 1 } alone of the form f(x1,h(x1))f ( x _ { 1 } , h ( x _ { 1 } ) ) . The maximum with respect to x1x _ { 1 } could then be found by differentiation in the usual way, to give the stationary value x1⋆x _ { 1 } ^ { \star } , with the corresponding value of x2x _ { 2 } given by x2⋆=h(x1⋆)x _ { 2 } ^ { \star } = h ( x _ { 1 } ^ { \star } )

One problem with this approach is that it may be difficult to find an analytic solution of the constraint equation that allows x2x _ { 2 } to be expressed as an explicit function of x1x _ { 1 } . Also, this approach treats x1x _ { 1 } and x2x _ { 2 } differently and so spoils the natural symmetry between these variables.

A more elegant, and often simpler, approach is based on the introduction of a parameter λ called a Lagrange multiplier. We shall motivate this technique from a geometrical perspective. Consider a D-dimensional variable x with components x1,…,xDx _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { D } . The constraint equation g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 then represents a (D−1)( D - 1 ) -dimensional surface in x-space as indicated in Figure E.1.

We first note that at any point on the constraint surface the gradient ∇g(𝐱)\nabla g ( \mathbf { x } ) of the constraint function will be orthogonal to the surface. To see this, consider a point x that lies on the constraint surface, and consider a nearby point 𝐱+ϵ\mathbf { x } + \epsilon that also lies on the surface. If we make a Taylor expansion around x, we have

g(𝐱+𝛜)≃g(𝐱)+𝛜T∇g(𝐱). g (\mathbf {x} + \boldsymbol {\epsilon}) \simeq g (\mathbf {x}) + \boldsymbol {\epsilon} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \nabla g (\mathbf {x}).\tag{E.2}

Because both x and 𝐱+ϵ\mathbf { x } + \epsilon lie on the constraint surface, we have g(𝐱)=g(𝐱+ϵ)g ( \mathbf { x } ) = g ( \mathbf { x } + \epsilon ) and hence ϵT∇g(𝐱)≃0\epsilon ^ { \mathrm { T } } \nabla g ( \mathbf { x } ) \simeq 0 . In the limit ∥ϵ∥0\| \epsilon \| 0 we have ϵT∇g(𝐱)=‾0\epsilon ^ { \mathrm { T } } \nabla g ( \mathbf { x } ) \bar { = } \mathrm { ~ 0 ~ } , and because  is

Figure E.1 A geometrical picture of the technique of Lagrange multipliers in which we seek to maximize a function f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) , subject to the constraint g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 If x is D dimensional, the constraint g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 corresponds to a subspace of dimensionality D−1D - 1 indicated by the red curve. The problem can be solved by optimizing the Lagrangian function L(𝐱,λ)=f(𝐱)+̇λg(𝐱)L ( \mathbf { x } , \lambda ) = f ( \mathbf { x } ) \dot { + } \lambda g ( \mathbf { x } )

then parallel to the constraint surface g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 , we see that the vector ∇g\nabla g is normal to the surface.

Next we seek a point 𝐱⋆\mathbf { x } ^ { \star } on the constraint surface such that f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) is maximized. Such a point must have the property that the vector ∇f(𝐱)\nabla f ( \mathbf { x } ) is also orthogonal to the constraint surface, as illustrated in Figure E.1, because otherwise we could increase the value of f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) by moving a short distance along the constraint surface. Thus ∇f\nabla f and ∇g\nabla g are parallel (or anti-parallel) vectors, and so there must exist a parameter λ such that

∇f+λ∇g=0 \nabla f + \lambda \nabla g = 0\tag{E.3}

where λ≠0\lambda \neq 0 is known as a Lagrange multiplier. Note that λ can have either sign.

At this point, it is convenient to introduce the Lagrangian function defined by

L(𝐱,λ)≡f(𝐱)+λg(𝐱). L (\mathbf {x}, \lambda) \equiv f (\mathbf {x}) + \lambda g (\mathbf {x}).\tag{E.4}

The constrained stationarity condition (E.3) is obtained by setting ∇𝐱L=0\nabla _ { \mathbf x } L = 0 . Furthermore, the condition $\partial { \cal L } / \partial \lambda = 0$ leads to the constraint equation g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0

Thus to find the maximum of a function f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) subject to the constraint g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 we define the Lagrangian function given by (E.4) and we then find the stationary point of L(𝐱,λ)L ( \mathbf { x } , \lambda ) with respect to both x and λ. For a D-dimensional vector x, this gives D+1D + 1 equations that determine both the stationary point 𝐱⋆\mathbf { x } ^ { \star } and the value of λ. If we are only interested in 𝐱⋆\mathbf { x } ^ { \star } , then we can eliminate λ from the stationarity equations without needing to find its value (hence the term ‘undetermined multiplier’).

As a simple example, suppose we wish to find the stationary point of the function f(x1,x2)=1⋅−x12−x⋅22f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = \overset { \cdot } { 1 } - x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } - \overset { \cdot } { x } _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } subject to the constraint g(x1,x2)=x1+x2−1=0g ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = x _ { 1 } + x _ { 2 } - 1 = 0 , as illustrated in Figure E.2. The corresponding Lagrangian function is given by

L(𝐱,λ)=1−x12−x22+λ(x1+x2−1). L (\mathbf {x}, \lambda) = 1 - x _ {1} ^ {2} - x _ {2} ^ {2} + \lambda (x _ {1} + x _ {2} - 1).\tag{E.5}

The conditions for this Lagrangian to be stationary with respect to x1,x2x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , and λ give the following coupled equations:

−2x1+λ=0 - 2 x _ {1} + \lambda = 0\tag{E.6}

−2x2+λ=0 - 2 x _ {2} + \lambda = 0\tag{E.7}

x1+x2−1=0. x _ {1} + x _ {2} - 1 = 0.\tag{E.8}

The circles show contours of the function f(x1,x2)f ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) , and the diagonal line shows the constraint surface g(x1,x2)=0‾g ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = \bar { 0 }

Solution of these equations then gives the stationary point as (x1⋆,x2⋆)=(12,12)\begin{array} { r } { ( x _ { 1 } ^ { \star } , x _ { 2 } ^ { \star } ) = ( \frac { 1 } { 2 } , \frac { 1 } { 2 } ) } \end{array} , and the corresponding value for the Lagrange multiplier is λ=1\lambda = 1

So far, we have considered the problem of maximizing a function subject to an equality constraint of the form g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 . We now consider the problem of maximizing f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) subject to an inequality constraint of the form g(𝐱)≥0g ( \mathbf { x } ) \geqslant 0 , as illustrated in Figure E.3.

There are now two kinds of solution possible, according to whether the constrained stationary point lies in the region where g(𝐱)>0g ( \mathbf { x } ) > 0 , in which case the constraint is inactive, or whether it lies on the boundary g(𝐱)=0g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 , in which case the constraint is said to be active. In the former case, the function g(𝐱)g ( \mathbf { x } ) plays no role and so the stationary condition is simply ∇f(𝐱)=0\nabla f ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 . This again corresponds to a stationary point of the Lagrange function (E.4) but this time with λ=0\lambda = 0 . The latter case, where the solution lies on the boundary, is analogous to the equality constraint discussed previously and corresponds to a stationary point of the Lagrange function (E.4) with λ≠0\lambda \neq 0 . Now, however, the sign of the Lagrange multiplier is crucial, because the function f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) will only be at a maximum if its gradient is oriented away from the region g(𝐱)>0g ( \mathbf { x } ) > 0 , as illustrated in Figure E.3. We therefore have ∇f(𝐱)=−λ∇g(𝐱)\nabla f ( \mathbf { x } ) = - \lambda \nabla g ( \mathbf { x } ) for some value of λ>0\lambda > 0

For either of these two cases, the product λg(𝐱)=0\lambda g ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 . Thus the solution to the problem of maximizing f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) subject to g(𝐱)≥0g ( \mathbf { x } ) ~ \geqslant ~ 0 is obtained by optimizing the Lagrange function (E.4) with respect to x and λ subject to the conditions

g(𝐱)≥0 g (\mathbf {x}) \geqslant 0

λ≥0 \lambda \geqslant 0\tag{E.9}

λg(𝐱)=0 \lambda g (\mathbf {x}) = 0\tag{E.10}

(E.11)

These are known as the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions (Karush, 1939; Kuhn and Tucker, 1951).

Note that if we wish to minimize (rather than maximize) the function f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) subject to an inequality constraint g(𝐱)≥0g ( \mathbf { x } ) \geqslant 0 , then we minimize the Lagrangian function L(𝐱,λ)=f(𝐱‾)−λg(𝐱)L ( \mathbf { x } , \lambda ) = f ( \mathbf { \bar { x } } ) - \lambda g ( \mathbf { x } ) with respect to x, again subject to λ≥0\lambda \geqslant 0

Finally, it is straightforward to extend the technique of Lagrange multipliers to the case of multiple equality and inequality constraints. Suppose we wish to maximize f(𝐱)f ( \mathbf { x } ) subject to gj(𝐱)=0for⁡j=1,…,J,g _ { j } ( \mathbf { x } ) = 0 \operatorname { f o r } j = 1 , \ldots , J , , and $h _ { k } ( { \bf x } ) \geqslant 0$ for k=1,…,Kk = 1 , \ldots , K We then introduce Lagrange multipliers {λj}\{ \lambda _ { j } \} and {μk}\{ \mu _ { k } \} , and then optimize the Lagrangian function given by

L(𝐱,{λj},{μk})=f(𝐱)+∑j=1Jλjgj(𝐱)+∑k=1Kμkhk(𝐱) L (\mathbf {x}, \{\lambda_ {j} \}, \{\mu_ {k} \}) = f (\mathbf {x}) + \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {J} \lambda_ {j} g _ {j} (\mathbf {x}) + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \mu_ {k} h _ {k} (\mathbf {x})\tag{E.12}

subject to μk≥0\mu _ { k } \geqslant 0 and $\mu _ { k } h _ { k } ( { \bf x } ) = 0$ for k=1,…,Kk = 1 , \ldots , K . Extensions to constrained functional derivatives are similarly straightforward. For a more detailed discussion of the technique of Lagrange multipliers, see Nocedal and Wright (1999).
